neutral_facts.value: The accused, a relative of the deceased, was alleged to have taken the deceased under a pretext and thereafter killed her. The deceased, who was married against her family's wishes, left with the accused on the day of the incident. The accused was arrested later, and some of the deceased's jewellery was recovered from his possession. The deceased's body was found with signs of asphyxia. The prosecution relied on the last seen evidence of witnesses, medical evidence, and the recovery of the jewellery. The accused's family had accepted the marriage, and a child was born to the couple, which cast doubt on the motive. The recovery of the jewellery was questioned as it was commonly available, and the accused was found in possession of it for over a week after the incident.

quotes.text: the trial court on a consideration of the evidence of P.W. 1, the first informant and the husband of the deceased, P.W. 2 the house owner in which the deceased and P.W. 1 were living, P.W. 3 the son of P.W. 2 who stated that he had gone to the telephone booth of P.W. 4 and had brought the appellant to their house on the 14th of August, 2002 and P.W. 4 the telephone booth owner who deposed to the fact that the appellant had come to the booth on the day in question where P.W. 3 had been waiting for him and thereafter gone along with him to the house of P.W. 2, P.W. 6 a press reporter and a colleague of P.W. 1 who had last seen the deceased and the appellant at the bus stand at Ravulapalem and as supported by the medical evidence and the recoveries of the ornaments from the appellant convicted him of the offences charged and sentenced him accordingly.

witness_credibility.value: The court assessed the main witnesses' credibility as uncertain, particularly noting the delayed recording of statements and lack of test identification parade.

quotes.text: the last seen evidence of P.Ws. 2, 3 and 6 is equally uncertain. Significantly, the statements of P.Ws.2 and 3 were recorded by the Magistrate for the first time under Section 164 about four months after the alleged incident and though both witnesses had deposed that they would be able to identify the appellant who was otherwise a stranger to them, no effort had been made to hold a test identification parade.

post_offence_conduct.value: The appellant continued to move around with the jewellery till its recovery from him on the 7th of September, 2002.

quotes.text: It is also completely unacceptable that though the incident happened on the 14th of August, 2002 the appellant had continued to move around with the jewellery still in his pocket till its recovery from him on the 7th of September, 2002.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant was connected to the crime through the last seen evidence of witnesses, medical evidence, and the recovery of the deceased's jewellery from the appellant's possession.

quotes.text: The trial court on a consideration of the evidence of P.W. 1, the first informant and the husband of the deceased, P.W. 2 the house owner in which the deceased and P.W. 1 were living, P.W. 3 the son of P.W. 2 who stated that he had gone to the telephone booth of P.W. 4 and had brought the appellant to their house on the 14th of August, 2002 and P.W. 4 the telephone booth owner who deposed to the fact that the appellant had come to the booth on the day in question where P.W. 3 had been waiting for him and thereafter gone along with him to the house of P.W. 2, P.W. 6 a press reporter and a colleague of P.W. 1 who had last seen the deceased and the appellant at the bus stand at Ravulapalem and as supported by the medical evidence and the recoveries of the ornaments from the appellant convicted him of the offences charged and sentenced him accordingly.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that there was no substantial evidence linking the appellant to the crime, the First Information Report was not a proper FIR, and the chain of circumstantial evidence was missing.

quotes.text: Mr. Siddharth Dave, the learned Amicus for the appellant, has submitted that there was absolutely no evidence to connect the appellant to the crime and the First Information Report recorded on the 18th August, 2002 was no FIR in the eyes of law as the first FIR recorded was that of a missing person on the 16th August, 2002 and in this report the first informant(P.W. 1) had not expressed his suspicion about the identify of the culprit.

He has also pointed out that except for the last seen evidence of P.Ws. 2, 3 and 6, there was no other evidence to connect the appellant with the murder as the recoveries alleged to have been made by the police on the 7th of September, 2002 could not be believed.

legal_principle_applied.value: The court applied the principle that in cases of circumstantial evidence, motive is a strong circumstance that must be proved by the prosecution, and the evidence must form a chain to establish guilt.

quotes.text: In a case relating to circumstantial evidence, motive is often a very strong circumstance which has to be proved by the prosecution and it is this circumstance which often forms the fulcrum of the prosecution story.
